evidence.source: RITES extract, page 8, 'Peak Hour Traffic - 2019 (Hebbal)': a turning diagram for the whole interchange (flyover, ramps and ground level together), in PCU per hour, total 26,896. The daily diagram on page 7 is dated July 2019. The page does not say which hour of the day the peak hour is.

IIT Bombay report, section 5.2 'Junction traffic volumes': Hebbal Junction, morning peak 09:00 to 10:00, 32,770 vehicles per hour = 31,758 PCU per hour, quoted from the tunnel project report's counts. The report gives no turning movements and no table of vehicle classes, and says signal timings were not recorded. The IISc review confirms the same figures and finds the report's base speed (13.74 km/h) at odds with the 4.29 km/h observed.

31,758 PCU / 32,770 vehicles at Hebbal Junction in the 09:00 to 10:00 peak (IIT Bombay report, section 5.2). Used to turn the 2019 RITES volumes from PCU into vehicles. An assumption because it joins two surveys years apart, and neither document says which PCU factors it used. The RITES 2051 forecast table implies 1.23 PCU per vehicle, with goods vehicles and buses included.

RITES 2019 peak-hour turning volumes (confirmed, above), divided by 0.969 PCU per vehicle (assumed, above) and put on the roads of the corridor by hand from the OpenStreetMap layout as it is in November 2026. The counts are from July 2019; the ramp from K.R. Puram towards the city opened after that, so which road each movement uses today is our reading of the map, not an observation.

groundLevel.note: Leaves the ground-level network at the foot of the loop; the loop and the ramp towards the city are raised.

needingTheFlyover.note: How it divides at the fork between the Ganga Nagar flyover and the ground-level road to the CBI Road junction is not published.

leftOut.note: Taken to use the loop flyover from the airport side to the Outer Ring Road eastbound (way 30213110), which is outside the extent. The published signal plan does give road A a left turn at ground level; how the movement divides between the two is not published.
Not city-bound: uses the airport-bound flyover and its ramps.

evidence.source: The flows above, put on the roads of the whole network. The published volume of each flow is kept in publishedVehiclesPerHour. The default demand of the corridor is each of them times defaultScale.value.

ASSUMED, no source: not published in anything read. Of the city-bound traffic at the fork ahead of the Ganga Nagar flyover, 80% is taken to go over the flyover, 10% straight on along the service road beyond the CBI Road junction, 5% left into CBI Road towards RT Nagar and 5% right beneath the flyover. Reason: the flyover has 3 lanes and the service road 2, and through traffic to the city has no reason to leave the flyover; the service road serves local destinations.

ASSUMED, no source: no count at the CBI Road junction was found. 300 vehicles per hour from RT Nagar along CBI Road, 200 of them on towards the city along the service road and 100 straight on beneath the flyover, so that the junction's second phase has traffic. A planner should set these when counts are known.

OUR CHOICE, not a measurement of traffic. The model cannot carry the published volumes: run for an hour in mixed traffic (seed 1, 2026-11-12), the published volumes (18,080 vehicles per hour on the corridor's roads) put 10,355 through, with 6,655 still waiting to enter at the end and the three Hebbal approaches full (394 m, 300 m and 299 m). The default demand is the published volumes times 0.3, the largest scale tried (in steps of 0.05) at which only one signal approach fills: the ground road from the airport, which has the least green (37 s of 160), peaks at 96 m of 394, and the Outer Ring Road from K.R. Puram at 63 m of 299. The Outer Ring Road from Tumkur Road fills its 300 m at every scale from 0.2 up, and not at 0.15. The assumed CBI Road flows are not scaled. Candidate reasons the model carries less than the counts: the signal plan dates from 2010 and the junction now runs other timings or adaptive control; the published plan gives green to movements and the network format to whole approaches, so A's left turn loses phase 3 and B's left turn phase 1, and C's right turn was added to phase 2 where it crosses B's straight traffic; vehicles do not sort by turn before the stop line and a later vehicle never goes before an earlier one; widths are lanes x 3.5 m, assumed; the volumes are 2019 counts in PCU turned into vehicles with an assumed 0.969, and which road each movement uses today is our reading of the map; the count may include movements outside the modelled roads; and the engine's junction discharge is not yet calibrated against a measured saturation flow. Use the demand scale control to try other levels, up to 1 for the published volumes.

RITES extract, page 26, 'Traffic Input for Horizon Year - Scenario 1', estimated traffic for 2051 in vehicles: car 8,354; taxi 6,266; two-wheeler 11,835; auto 2,437; bus (private, KSRTC) 1,044; LCV 1,392; truck 1,741; multi-axle 696; total 33,765. This is a forecast input, not an observed mix: no document read gives an observed count by vehicle class at Hebbal (the pie chart on page 6 is a 2019 split of trips by mode: public transport 45%, car and taxi 36%, two-wheeler 16%, auto 3%). Car and taxi are counted together as car; goods vehicles (3,829, 11% of vehicles) are left out because the engine has no class for them; the 728 BMTC buses per hour given separately are left out.
